Os verbos reflexivos e os pronomes me, t: Reflexive verbs and the pronouns me, te, se, nos, os, se
PASSO 1: um verbo reflexivo é aquele em: STEP 1: a reflexive verb is one where the action comes back onto the person doing it: I wash myself, I get myself up. In the infinitive it ends in «-se»: «levantarse», «ducharse». STEP 2: in a sentence, each person has its own pronoun, placed BEFORE the conjugated verb: me levanto, te levantas, se levanta, nos levantamos, os levantáis, se levantan. STEP 3: the pronoun agrees with the subject: «Yo me levanto», «Nosotros nos levantamos». You can't say «yo se levanta». STEP 4: «ducharse» and «lavarse» are regular. But some reflexives change their stem vowel, as you saw in lesson 13: acostarse (me acuesto), despertarse (me despierto), dormirse (me duermo) and, with e → i, vestirse (me visto, te vistes, se viste, nos vestimos, os vestís, se visten). STEP 5: with a second verb, the pronoun can go either before the conjugated verb or stuck onto the infinitive, with no hyphen: «Me quiero levantar» or «Quiero levantarme»; «Tengo que ducharme» or «Me tengo que duchar». Pick whichever sounds more natural to you. STEP 6: with a negative, «no» comes before the pronoun: «No me levanto temprano». STEP 7: body parts and clothes take the article, not the possessive: «Me lavo las manos», «Me peino el pelo». STEP 8: many verbs change meaning with the pronoun: «lavar» (to wash something) versus «lavarse» (to wash oneself); «acostar» (to put someone else to bed) versus «acostarse» (to go to bed oneself); «dormir» (to sleep) versus «dormirse» (to fall asleep).
em português também há verbos pronominai: English also marks reflexive action with a pronoun, but it comes AFTER the verb and is often dropped or replaced by context («I get up», not «I get myself up»; «I wake up», not «I wake myself up»). In Spanish the pronoun is required and always comes BEFORE the conjugated verb: «me levanto», never «levanto» alone. Without it, the sentence is wrong or changes its meaning entirely.
I wake up at seven thirty.
My brother goes to sleep very late.
I don't get up early on Sundays.

Contar o dia: sequência, horas e frequên: Narrating your day: sequence, clock time, and frequency
PASSO 1: para ordenar as ações, use «pri: STEP 1: to put actions in order, use «primero» (first), «luego» or «después» (then, afterward), «por último» (finally). After «antes de» and «después de», the verb stays in the infinitive: «Antes de salir, desayuno» (before leaving, I have breakfast), «Después de cenar, veo la tele» (after dinner, I watch TV). STEP 2: clock times follow lesson 9's pattern: «a las ocho». With the exact hour, say «de la mañana», «de la tarde» or «de la noche»: «a las ocho de la mañana». Without a specific hour, use «por la mañana», «por la tarde», «por la noche»: «Estudio por la tarde». STEP 3: the trap: «la mañana» means morning, and «mañana» (with no article) means tomorrow. «Mañana por la mañana» means «tomorrow morning». STEP 4: frequency words: «todos los días» (every day), «casi siempre» (almost always), «normalmente» (usually), «a menudo» (often), «de vez en cuando» (now and then), «nunca» (never). Fixed days of the week take the article: «los lunes» (on Mondays), «los fines de semana» (on weekends). STEP 5: mealtimes. In Spain, the main midday meal tends to be later than it is in Brazil, and it's commonly called «comer» (la comida); «almorzar» is also heard. In Latin America, «almorzar» and «el almuerzo» are the usual words. «Desayunar» is to have breakfast, and «cenar» is to have dinner. «Merendar» is to have an afternoon snack. STEP 6: «almorzar» changes o → ue (almuerzo, almuerzas…), and the «z» becomes «c» only before «e». «Empezar» changes e → ie: «Empiezo a trabajar a las nueve» (I start work at nine). «Volver» changes o → ue: «Vuelvo a casa a las seis» (I get back home at six). STEP 7: false friend: «la cena» means dinner. A scene from a movie is «la escena», and the Christmas Eve dinner is «la cena de Nochebuena».
em português «manhã» e «amanhã» são pala: English «dinner» can mean the main meal at any hour, which can be at noon in some dialects — Spanish keeps the midday meal and the evening meal as two separate words (comida/almuerzo versus cena) in every region. And where English «scene» and the word for an evening meal sound nothing alike, Spanish «cena» (dinner) and «escena» (scene) look deceptively similar on the page, which is exactly why it's flagged here as a false friend.

Ponerse, quedarse, irse, sentirse e a aç: Ponerse, quedarse, irse, sentirse, and reciprocal action
PASSO 1: «ponerse» significa colocar alg: STEP 1: «ponerse» means to put something on yourself: «Me pongo el abrigo» (I put my coat on). To take it off, «quitarse»: «Me quito los zapatos» (I take my shoes off). STEP 2: «quedarse» means to stay somewhere: «Me quedo en casa» (I'm staying home). Watch out: «quedar» without the pronoun can mean to arrange to meet («Quedamos a las ocho»); with «se», it means to stay put. STEP 3: «irse» means to leave, to go away from where you are: «Me voy» (I'm leaving), «Nos vamos a casa» (we're heading home). Without the pronoun, «ir» just points to a destination: «Voy a casa» (I'm going home). STEP 4: «sentirse» + bien/mal/cansado: «Me siento bien» (I feel fine), «Se siente cansada» (she feels tired). The verb changes e → ie: me siento, te sientes, se siente, nos sentimos, os sentís, se sienten. STEP 5: when two or more people do the action to each other, the plural pronoun carries the sense of «to one another»: «Nos llamamos todos los días» (we call each other every day), «Se escriben mucho» (they write to each other a lot). STEP 6: if a sentence could be ambiguous (for example, «se miran» could mean «they look at themselves» or «they look at each other»), context settles it; to make the reciprocal meaning explicit, you can add «el uno al otro».
em português, «ir» e «ir-se» se distingu: English «to leave» and «to go» are two separate verbs, so the distinction feels familiar — but in Spanish it's the SAME verb, «ir», with the pronoun doing all the work: «me voy» is «I'm leaving / heading off», and «voy» alone is just «I'm going (somewhere)». The reciprocal sense, as in «nos vemos» (we see each other, see you around), has no separate verb in English either — English reaches for «each other» as separate words, where Spanish folds it straight into the pronoun.
